problems.question: What value of \(x\) satisfies \[x- \frac{3}{4} = \frac{5}{12} - \frac{1}{3}?\]
hints: First simplify the right side using denominator \(12\)
After finding the right side, add \(\frac34\) to both sides
problems.solution: The right side is \(\dfrac{5}{12}-\dfrac13=\dfrac{5}{12}-\dfrac4{12}=\dfrac1{12}\). Thus \(x=\dfrac34+\dfrac1{12}=\dfrac9{12}+\dfrac1{12}=\dfrac56\). Thus, E is the correct answer.

problems.question: The numbers \(3,\) \(5,\) \(7,\) \(a,\) and \(b\) have an average (arithmetic mean) of \(15.\) What is the average of \(a\) and \(b?\)
hints: Convert the average of five numbers into a total sum
Subtract the known three numbers before averaging \(a\) and \(b\)
problems.solution: The five numbers have total sum \(5\cdot15=75\). Since \(3+5+7=15\), we have \(a+b=75-15=60\), so the average of \(a\) and \(b\) is \(30\). Thus, C is the correct answer.

problems.question:
Assuming \(a
eq3,\) \(b
eq4,\) and \(c
eq5,\) what is the value in simplest form of the following expression? \[ rac{a-3}{5-c} \cdot  rac{b-4}{3-a} \cdot  rac{c-5}{4-b}\]
hints: Each denominator is the negative of a matching numerator factor
Count the number of negative signs after cancellation
problems.solution: Rewrite the denominator factors as \(5-c=-(c-5)\), \(3-a=-(a-3)\), and \(4-b=-(b-4)\). The expression becomes \(\dfrac{(a-3)(b-4)(c-5)}{-(a-3)(b-4)(c-5)}=-1\). Thus, A is the correct answer.

problems.question: A driver travels for \(2\) hours at \(60\) miles per hour, during which her car gets \(30\) miles per gallon of gasoline. She is paid \(\$0.50\) per mile, and her only expense is gasoline at \(\$2.00\) per gallon. What is her net rate of pay, in dollars per hour, after this expense?
hints: Find the total miles driven in two hours
Subtract gasoline cost before dividing by the number of hours
problems.solution: The driver travels \(2\cdot60=120\) miles, so she is paid \(120\cdot \$0.50=\$60\). The trip uses \(\frac{120}{30}=4\) gallons of gasoline, costing \(4\cdot\$2=\$8\). Her net pay is \(60-8=52\) dollars over \(2\) hours, or \(26\) dollars per hour. Thus, E is the correct answer.

problems.question: What is the sum of all real numbers \(x\) for which \[|x^2-12x+34|=2?\]
hints: Split the absolute-value equation into two quadratic equations
Remember to count the double root only once in the sum of real numbers
problems.solution: The equation means \(x^2-12x+34=2\) or \(x^2-12x+34=-2\). The first gives \(x^2-12x+32=0\), with roots \(4\) and \(8\). The second gives \((x-6)^2=0\), with root \(6\). The sum of all real solutions is \(4+8+6=18\). Thus, C is the correct answer.

problems.question: How many \(4\)-digit positive integers (that is, integers between \(1000\) and \(9999,\) inclusive) having only even digits are divisible by \(5?\)
hints: The last digit must be compatible with both evenness and divisibility by \(5\)
Choose the thousands, hundreds, and tens digits independently after fixing the last digit
problems.solution: The last digit must be \(0\), because the number is divisible by \(5\) and all digits are even. The thousands digit can be \(2,4,6,\) or \(8\), and each of the hundreds and tens digits has \(5\) choices. Thus there are \(4\cdot5\cdot5=100\) such integers. Thus, B is the correct answer.

problems.question: The \(25\) integers from \(-10\) to \(14,\) inclusive, can be arranged to form a \(5\)-by-\(5\) square in which the sum of the numbers in each row, the sum of the numbers in each column, and the sum of the numbers along each of the main diagonals are all the same. What is the value of this common sum?
hints: The five row sums together equal the sum of all \(25\) integers
Compute the arithmetic-sequence sum from \(-10\) through \(14\)
problems.solution: The sum of the integers from \(-10\) to \(14\) is \(25\cdot\dfrac{-10+14}{2}=50\). If every row has common sum \(S\), then the five row sums add to \(50\), so \(5S=50\) and \(S=10\). Thus, C is the correct answer.

problems.question: What is the value of \[ \begin{aligned} &1+2+3-4+5+6+7-8\\ &\quad+\cdots\\ &\quad+197+198+199-200? \end{aligned} \]
hints: Group the expression into blocks of four terms
Find a formula for the \(j\)th block and sum over \(50\) blocks
problems.solution: Group the terms in blocks of four: \((1+2+3-4)\) \(+(5+6+7-8)\) \(+\cdots\) \(+(197+198+199-200)\). The \(j\)th block is \((4j-3)+(4j-2)\) \(+(4j-1)-4j=8j-6\). There are \(50\) blocks, so the sum is \(\sum_{j=1}^{50}(8j-6)=8\cdot\dfrac{50\cdot51}{2}\) \(-6\cdot50=9900\). Thus, B is the correct answer.

problems.question: A single bench section at a school event can hold either \(7\) adults or \(11\) children. When \(N\) bench sections are connected end to end, an equal number of adults and children seated together will occupy all the bench space. What is the least possible positive integer value of \(N?\)
hints: Let the equal number of adults and children be \(P\)
The number of bench sections is \(\frac{P}{7}+\frac{P}{11}\)
problems.solution: If the equal number of adults and children is \(P\), then the adults use \(\frac{P}{7}\) bench sections and the children use \(\frac{P}{11}\) bench sections. Thus \(N=P\left(\dfrac17+\dfrac1{11}\right)=\dfrac{18P}{77}\). The least positive integer occurs when \(P=77\), giving \(N=18\). Thus, B is the correct answer.

problems.question: Seven cubes, whose volumes are \(1,\) \(8,\) \(27,\) \(64,\) \(125,\) \(216,\) and \(343\) cubic units, are stacked vertically to form a tower in which the volumes of the cubes decrease from bottom to top. Except for the bottom cube, the bottom face of each cube lies completely on top of the cube below it. What is the total surface area of the tower (including the bottom) in square units?
hints: Start with the surface areas of all seven separate cubes
Each contact hides two faces with the side length of the smaller cube
problems.solution: The cube side lengths are \(1,2,3,4,5,6,7\), stacked from largest on bottom to smallest on top. The sum of the surface areas of the separate cubes is \(6(1^2+2^2+\cdots+7^2)\) \(=6\cdot140=840\). Each contact hides two square faces, with areas \(1^2,2^2,\ldots,6^2\). Subtracting these hidden faces gives \(840\) \(-2(1^2+2^2+\cdots+6^2)\) \(=840-182=658\). Thus, B is the correct answer.

problems.question: What is the median of the following list of \(4040\) numbers? \[ \begin{aligned} &1,2,3,\ldots,2020,\\ &1^2,2^2,3^2,\ldots,2020^2 \end{aligned} \]
hints: Near the median, count ordinary integers and square numbers separately
problems.solution: For a number near the median, the sorted list includes all ordinary integers up to that number and all squares up to that number. Since \(44^2=1936\) and \(45^2=2025\), there are \(44\) squares not exceeding any number from \(1936\) through \(2020\). At \(1975\), there are \(1975+44=2019\) list entries at most \(1975\). At \(1976\), there are \(2020\) entries at most \(1976\), so the \(2020\)th entry is \(1976\), and the next is \(1977\). The median is \(1976.5\). Thus, C is the correct answer.

problems.question: Triangle \(AMC\) is isosceles with \(AM = AC.\) Medians \(\overline{MV}\) and \(\overline{CU}\) are perpendicular to each other, and \(MV=CU=12.\) What is the area of \(\triangle AMC?\)
hints: Put the centroid at the origin and align the perpendicular medians with the axes
The centroid divides each median in a \(2:1\) ratio
problems.solution: Let the centroid be the origin. Since a centroid divides each median in a \(2:1\) ratio, we may place median \(MV\) horizontally with \(M=(8,0)\) and \(V=(-4,0)\), and median \(CU\) vertically with \(C=(0,8)\) and \(U=(0,-4)\). Because \(U\) is the midpoint of \(AM\), we get \(A=2U-M=(-8,-8)\). The area of \(\triangle AMC\) is \(\dfrac12 |(16,8)\times(8,16)|\) \(=\dfrac12(256-64)=96\). Thus, C is the correct answer.

problems.question: A frog sitting at the point \((1, 2)\) begins a sequence of jumps, where each jump is parallel to one of the coordinate axes and has length \(1,\) and the direction of each jump (up, down, right, or left) is chosen independently at random. The sequence ends when the frog reaches a side of the square with vertices \((0, 0),\) \((0, 4),\) \((4, 4),\) and \((4, 0).\) What is the probability that the sequence of jumps ends on a vertical side of the square?
hints: Let each interior lattice point store the probability of hitting a vertical side first
Use symmetry to reduce the random-walk equations to four unknowns
problems.solution: Let \(p(x,y)\) be the probability of eventually hitting a vertical side first from point \((x,y)\). By symmetry, set \(a=p(1,1)=p(1,3)\), \(b=p(2,1)=p(2,3)\), \(c=p(1,2)\), and \(d=p(2,2)\). The averaging equations are \(a=\dfrac{1+b+c}{4}\), \(b=\dfrac{2a+d}{4}\), \(c=\dfrac{1+2a+d}{4}\), and \(d=\dfrac{b+c}{2}\). Solving gives \(c=\dfrac58\), which is the desired probability from \((1,2)\). Thus, B is the correct answer.

problems.question: Real numbers \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy \(x + y = 4\) and \(x \cdot y = -2.\) What is the value of \[x + \frac{x^3}{y^2} + \frac{y^3}{x^2} + y?\]
hints: Use power sums \(S_k=x^k+y^k\)
The relation \(t^2-4t-2=0\) gives a recurrence for \(S_k\)
problems.solution: Let \(S_k=x^k+y^k\). Since \(x+y=4\) and \(xy=-2\), the numbers \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy \(t^2-4t-2=0\), so \(S_k=4S_{k-1}+2S_{k-2}\). Using \(S_0=2\) and \(S_1=4\), we get \(S_2=20\), \(S_3=88\), \(S_4=392\), and \(S_5=1744\). The expression is \(x+y+\dfrac{x^5+y^5}{x^2y^2}\) \(=4+\dfrac{1744}{4}=440\). Thus, D is the correct answer.

problems.question: A positive integer divisor of \(12!\) is chosen at random. The probability that the divisor chosen is a perfect square can be expressed as \(\frac{m}{n},\) where \(m\) and \(n\) are relatively prime positive integers. What is \(m+n?\)
hints: Factor \(12!\) into primes
A square divisor must choose only even prime exponents
problems.solution: The prime factorization of \(12!\) is \(2^{10}3^5 5^2 7^1 11^1\). Therefore \(12!\) has \((10+1)(5+1)\) \(\cdot(2+1)(1+1)(1+1)=792\) positive divisors. A square divisor must use only even exponents, giving \(6\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1\cdot1=36\) square divisors. The probability is \(\frac{36}{792}=\frac{1}{22}\), so \(m+n=1+22=23\). Thus, E is the correct answer.

problems.question: A point is chosen at random within the square in the coordinate plane whose vertices are \((0, 0),\) \((2020, 0),\) \((2020, 2020),\) and \((0, 2020).\) The probability that the point is within \(d\) units of a lattice point is \(\tfrac{1}{2}.\) (A point \((x, y)\) is a lattice point if \(x\) and \(y\) are both integers.) What is \(d\) to the nearest tenth?
hints: Look at one unit square of the lattice
The four quarter-circles around its corners have total area \(\pi d^2\)
problems.solution: For \(d<\dfrac12\), the points within \(d\) of lattice points occupy, in each unit square, four quarter-circles whose total area is \(\pi d^2\). The enormous square is tiled by unit squares, so the desired probability is \(\pi d^2\). Setting \(\pi d^2=\dfrac12\) gives \(d=\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{2\pi}}\approx0.399\), which rounds to \(0.4\). Thus, B is the correct answer.

problems.question: Define \[ \begin{aligned} P(x)={}&(x-1^2)(x-2^2)\\ &\cdots(x-100^2). \end{aligned} \] How many integers \(n\) are there such that \(P(n)\leq 0?\)
hints: Make a sign chart across the square roots \(1^2,2^2,\ldots,100^2\)
Count integer points in every other interval, including endpoints
problems.solution: The polynomial changes sign at each square \(1^2,2^2,\ldots,100^2\), and its leading coefficient is positive. Thus \(P(n)\le0\) for integers in the intervals \([1^2,2^2]\), \([3^2,4^2]\), \(\ldots\), \([99^2,100^2]\). For odd \(k\), the interval \([k^2,(k+1)^2]\) contains \((k+1)^2-k^2+1=2k+2\) integers. Summing over odd \(k=1,3,\ldots,99\) gives \(2(1+3+\cdots+99)\) \(+2\cdot50=5000+100\) \(=5100\). Thus, E is the correct answer.

problems.question: Let \((a,b,c,d)\) be an ordered quadruple of not necessarily distinct integers, each one of them in the set \(\{0,1,2,3\}.\) For how many such quadruples is it true that \(a\cdot d-b\cdot c\) is odd? (For example, \((0,3,1,1)\) is one such quadruple, because \(0\cdot 1-3\cdot 1 = -3\) is odd.)
hints: Only the parities of \(a,b,c,d\) matter
Count invertible \(2\times2\) matrices over the two-element field
problems.solution: Only parity matters. Modulo \(2\), the condition is that \(ad-bc\) is \(1\), meaning the matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}\) is invertible over \(\mathbb F_2\). There are \((4-1)(4-2)=6\) invertible \(2\times2\) matrices over \(\mathbb F_2\). Each parity pattern lifts to \(2^4=16\) choices from \(\{0,1,2,3\}\), so there are \(6\cdot16=96\) quadruples. Thus, C is the correct answer.

problems.question: As shown in the figure below, a regular dodecahedron (the polyhedron consisting of \(12\) congruent regular pentagonal faces) floats in space with two horizontal faces. Note that there is a ring of five slanted faces adjacent to the top face, and a ring of five slanted faces adjacent to the bottom face. How many ways are there to move from the top face to the bottom face via a sequence of adjacent faces so that each face is visited at most once and moves are not permitted from the bottom ring to the top ring?
hints: Because upward moves are forbidden, split every path into a top-ring phase and a bottom-ring phase
On a five-cycle, a self-avoiding walk has \(1+2\cdot4\) possible stopping paths
problems.solution: After leaving the top face, choose one of the \(5\) top-ring faces. Because moves from the bottom ring to the top ring are forbidden, every valid path has a top-ring phase, then one move down to the bottom ring, then a bottom-ring phase. Fix the first top-ring face. On the top ring, the path can move around the \(5\)-cycle without revisiting a face and then stop at any point: there are \(1+2\cdot4=9\) possible top-ring paths. From the stopping face, there are \(2\) possible downward moves to the bottom ring, so the top part has \(18\) choices. Once in the bottom ring, the path can move around the bottom \(5\)-cycle without revisiting a face and then enter the bottom face; this gives \(1+2\cdot4=9\) choices. The total is \(5\cdot18\cdot9=810\). Thus, E is the correct answer.

problems.question: Quadrilateral \(ABCD\) satisfies \(\angle ABC = \angle ACD = 90^{\circ},\) \(AC=20,\) and \(CD=30.\) Diagonals \(\overline{AC}\) and \(\overline{BD}\) intersect at point \(E,\) and \(AE=5.\) What is the area of quadrilateral \(ABCD?\)
hints: Put \(AC\) on the \(x\)-axis and use the known point \(E\)
Point \(B\) lies both on line \(DE\) and on the circle with diameter \(AC\)
problems.solution: Place \(A=(0,0)\) and \(C=(20,0)\). Since \(\angle ACD=90^\circ\) and \(CD=30\), take \(D=(20,30)\). The point \(E\) is \((5,0)\), so line \(BD\) has equation \(y=2(x-5)\). Because \(\angle ABC=90^\circ\), point \(B\) lies on the circle with diameter \(AC\): \((x-10)^2+y^2=100\). Intersecting with \(y=2(x-5)\) gives \(x=2\) or \(10\). The convex quadrilateral uses \(B=(2,-6)\). Then \([ACD]=\dfrac12\cdot20\cdot30=300\), and \([ABC]=\dfrac12\cdot20\cdot6=60\). The total area is \(360\). Thus, D is the correct answer.

problems.question: There exists a unique strictly increasing sequence of nonnegative integers \(a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_k\) such that \[\frac{2^{289}+1}{2^{17}+1}=2^{a_1}+2^{a_2}+\cdots+2^{a_k}.\] What is \(k?\)
hints: Pair positive and negative powers to create blocks of binary ones
problems.solution: Let \(X=2^{17}\). Then \[ \begin{gathered} \dfrac{2^{289}+1}{2^{17}+1} = \dfrac{X^{17}+1}{X+1} \\ = X^{16}-X^{15}+X^{14} \\ {}-\cdots-X+1 \end{gathered} \]. Pair consecutive terms: \(X^{16}-X^{15}\), \(X^{14}-X^{13}\), \(\ldots\), \(X^2-X\), and then the final \(+1\). Each pair is \(2^{17m}(2^{17}-1)\), contributing \(17\) ones in binary. There are \(8\) such pairs plus the final \(1\), so \(k=8\cdot17+1=137\). Thus, C is the correct answer.

problems.question: For how many positive integers \(n \le 1000\) is\[\left\lfloor \dfrac{998}{n} \right\rfloor+\left\lfloor \dfrac{999}{n} \right\rfloor+\left\lfloor \dfrac{1000}{n}\right \rfloor\]not divisible by \(3?\) (Recall that \(\lfloor x \rfloor\) is the greatest integer less than or equal to \(x.\))
hints: The sum of floors fails to be a multiple of \(3\) only when subtracting \(1\) or \(2\) crosses a multiple of \(n\)
problems.solution: Write \(1000=qn+r\), where \(0\le r<n\). Then \(\left\lfloor\dfrac{1000}{n}\right\rfloor=q\). The other two floors are usually also \(q\), except that subtracting \(1\) or \(2\) from \(1000\) crosses a multiple of \(n\) when \(r\) is small. For \(n>1\), the sum is not divisible by \(3\) exactly when \(r=0\) or \(r=1\). The case \(r=0\) gives divisors of \(1000\), excluding \(1\), for \(15\) values. The case \(r=1\) gives divisors of \(999\), excluding \(1\), for \((3+1)(1+1)-1=7\) values. The total is \(22\). Thus, A is the correct answer.

problems.question: Let \(T\) be the triangle in the coordinate plane with vertices \((0,0),\) \((4,0),\) and \((0,3).\) Consider the following five isometries (rigid transformations) of the plane: rotations of \(90^{\circ},\) \(180^{\circ},\) and \(270^{\circ}\) counterclockwise around the origin, reflection across the \(x\)-axis, and reflection across the \(y\)-axis. How many of the \(125\) sequences of three of these transformations (not necessarily distinct) will return \(T\) to its original position? (For example, a \(180^{\circ}\) rotation, followed by a reflection across the \(x\)-axis, followed by a reflection across the \(y\)-axis will return \(T\) to its original position, but a \(90^{\circ}\) rotation, followed by a reflection across the \(x\)-axis, followed by another reflection across the \(x\)-axis will not return \(T\) to its original position.)
hints: Name the \(90^\circ\) rotation \(R\) and the two reflections \(X,Y\)
Once the first two transformations are fixed, the third must be the inverse of their product
problems.solution: Let \(R\) be a \(90^\circ\) rotation, so the allowed rotations are \(R,R^2,R^3\). Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be the reflections across the coordinate axes. Once the first two transformations are chosen, the third is forced to be the inverse of their product. Among two rotations, \(6\) ordered pairs have a nonidentity rotation as their product. A rotation and a reflection have an allowed axis-reflection as their product exactly when the rotation is \(R^2\), giving \(4\) ordered pairs. Finally, the two different axis-reflections can occur in either order, giving \(2\) more pairs. Altogether there are \(6+4+2=12\) valid sequences. Thus, A is the correct answer.

problems.question: Let \(n\) be the least positive integer greater than \(1000\) for which \[ \begin{gathered} \gcd(63,n+120)=21\\ \text{and}\\ \gcd(n+63,120)=60. \end{gathered} \] What is the sum of the digits of \(n?\)
hints: Translate each gcd condition into a congruence plus an exclusion
Solve the two congruences first, then test candidates above \(1000\)
problems.solution: The first gcd condition gives \(n+120\equiv0\pmod{21}\), so \(n\equiv6\pmod{21}\), but \(n+120\) must not be divisible by \(63\). The second gives \(n+63\equiv0\pmod{60}\), so \(n\equiv57\pmod{60}\), but \(n+63\) must not be divisible by \(120\). Solving \(n\equiv6\pmod{21}\) and \(n\equiv57\pmod{60}\) gives \(n\equiv237\pmod{420}\). The candidates above \(1000\) are \(1077,1497,1917,\ldots\). The first fails the first gcd condition, the second fails the second gcd condition, and \(1917\) works. The digit sum is \(18\). Thus, C is the correct answer.

problems.question: Jason rolls three fair standard six-sided dice. Then he looks at the rolls and chooses a subset of the dice (possibly empty, possibly all three dice) to reroll. After rerolling, he wins if and only if the sum of the numbers face up on the three dice is exactly \(7.\) Jason always plays to optimize his chances of winning. What is the probability that he chooses to reroll exactly two of the dice?
hints: Compare the best chance from rerolling \(0,1,2,\) or \(3\) dice
Rerolling two dice is optimal only for certain sorted initial rolls with large two-smallest sum
problems.solution: For any initial roll, Jason compares the best probabilities from rerolling \(0,1,2,\) or \(3\) dice. Rerolling all three dice has probability \(\frac{15}{216}=\frac{5}{72}\). Rerolling one die has probability \(\frac{1}{6}\) whenever some pair of kept dice has sum at most \(6\). If he rerolls exactly two dice, he keeps one die. Keeping a die showing \(1,2,3,4,5,6\) gives probabilities \(5,4,3,2,1,0\) out of \(36\), respectively. This can be optimal only when the two smallest dice sum at least \(7\) and the smallest die is \(1,2,\) or \(3\). The sorted rolls satisfying this are \((1,6,6)\), \((2,5,5),(2,5,6),(2,6,6)\), and \((3,4,4),\) \((3,4,5),\) \((3,4,6),\) \((3,5,5),\) \((3,5,6),\) \((3,6,6)\). Counting permutations gives \(3+12+27=42\) rolls out of \(216\), so the probability is \(\frac{42}{216}=\frac{7}{36}\). Thus, A is the correct answer.
